verified_metadata.title: The relationship between building and urban mobility-based energy consumption and urban form: A machine learning approach
verified_metadata.abstract: Urban energy consumption studies predominantly focus on building energy use. However, urban form has the potential to influence energy consumption not only through building morphology but also through mobility demands shaped by spatial location within the city. In different locational contexts such as central, peripheral, coastal, and transitional zones, urban form varies in terms of density, building layout, and accessibility, which affects both building-related and trip-related energy demand. Despite this, studies that jointly evaluate the combined effects of urban morphological characteristics and locational mobility dynamics on energy consumption remain limited. Addressing this gap, this study assumes that urban energy consumption should be examined not only at the building scale but also in an integrated manner with the locational characteristics of urban form. Within this framework, urban forms in Istanbul were classified into seven categories using the k-means clustering algorithm. Subsequently, a dataset consisting of morphological variables derived from 32,112 buildings was modeled to predict building energy consumption. Among ten machine learning techniques, Random Forest was identified as the most successful algorithm, achieving an R² value of 0.87. The effects of urban morphological variables were interpreted using SHapley Additive Explanations. In the next step, energy consumption resulting from trips between Traffic Analysis Zones across different transportation modes was calculated. When building-related and trip-related energy consumption were evaluated together, Open low rise was identified as the least efficient form with an average energy consumption of 186 kWh/year·m², while Open skyscraper was identified as the most efficient form with an average of 85 kWh/year·m². However, when areas dominated by building energy and those dominated by trip-related energy were examined, it was observed that the energy performance of urban forms varied depending on spatial context. The findings provide insights to inform energy-oriented urban planning and urban design approaches.

verified_metadata.title: Collaboratively optimize of multi-scale spatial form within urban blocks for low-carbon performance: A machine learning-driven design support framework
verified_metadata.abstract: Achieving carbon-neutral city goals requires leveraging performance-based design in the early stages of planning. However, performance-driven multi-scale spatial form optimization for building carbon emissions has not yet been fully investigated. This disconnect presents a critical barrier to developing sustainable urban blocks. To bridge this gap, this study develops and validates a machine learning-driven framework to support the collaborative optimization of multi-scale spatial form for superior carbon performance. Taking office blocks in Wuhan as a case study, a parametric model was developed based on 50 real-world examples to ensure linked changes in spatial form of block and building scale. This model was used to generate a large dataset for training ensemble learning algorithms to rapidly predict and balance three key sustainability indicators: building energy carbon emissions (BECE), solar energy carbon reduction (SECR), and net carbon emissions (NCE). The framework demonstrates significant potential, compared with the simulation method, the proposed method can accelerate 150–160 times, informed decision-making for planners. The resulting optimized design solutions achieved an average 11.53 % reduction in BECE and an 79.34 % reduction in NCE compared to initial schemes. Using explainable AI (SHAP), the analysis overcomes the "black box" problem of machine learning models, identifying plot ratio and building density as the most critical parameters influencing net emissions and offering clear, actionable guidance for designers. This research provides a powerful, data-driven support tool for architects and urban planners to integrate carbon performance assessment into the formative stages of urban design. By offering a rapid and intelligent method for generating and evaluating low-carbon block configurations, this framework contributes directly to the creation of more sustainable, resilient, and climate-responsive cities.

verified_metadata.title: Impacts of grey-green spatial patterns on carbon emissions and sequestration in expanding and shrinking cities: An explainable machine learning approach
verified_metadata.abstract: Rapid urbanization and the rush to meet global climate commitments require a clearer understanding of how urban form drives carbon emissions (CE) and carbon sequestration (CS), here represented by net primary productivity (NPP) as a proxy for vegetation-driven carbon uptake. While existing research confirms that spatial morphology shapes CE and CS, it offers limited insight into how these relationships shift across different stages of urban development. In this study, we examine Chengdu and Harbin as representative expanding and shrinking cities and apply machine learning models integrated with Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) to identify the nonlinear effects of grey-green spatial patterns on urban carbon dynamics. Our results show that in expanding cities, structural attributes of grey space dominate CE patterns, whereas green space coverage and connectivity play a decisive role in strengthening CS. In shrinking cities, grey space characteristics largely govern both CE and CS. We also find that expanding cities respond more strongly to variations in spatial agglomeration and grey-green morphological coupling, displaying broader and more elastic emission-reduction and sequestration-enhancement ranges, whereas shrinking cities exhibit more constrained yet stable responses. Moreover, expanding cities reveal a marked synergistic effect when agglomeration and connectivity improve simultaneously, producing concurrent declines in CE and gains in CS. These findings underscore the threshold sensitivity and city-type specificity of grey-green spatial influences on the urban carbon cycle and offer evidence-based guidance for designing differentiated spatial optimization strategies that enhance sequestration and curb emissions in cities undergoing different development trajectories.

verified_metadata.title: A machine learning-based mediation analysis of urban form influences on building energy use: evidence from Seoul, South Korea
verified_metadata.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms through which urban contextual form influences building energy use is critical for developing accurate urban building energy models. However, few studies have examined the mechanisms that mediate the effect of urban form on building energy use. This study investigates three mediating mechanisms that link urban form to building energy use: solar insolation, contextual temperature, and occupant behavior. Using monthly energy use of residential plots in Seoul, South Korea, the study estimates mediation effects in summer and winter seasons. An artificial neural network (ANN) mediation model is trained to capture nonlinearity and interactions in the relationship and compared to traditional linear mediation models. Results suggest the ANN-based method has a higher accuracy and enhanced interpretability. Analyses show that contextual temperature is the dominant mediator for summer electricity and winter energy uses, with effects of 24-54%, while solar insolation also plays a major mediating role, with effects up to 47% in winter electricity. Occupant behavior mediates approximately 2-5% of urban form's effects on seasonal energy uses. Although modest, these effects are significant for green and water cover. Notably, significant residual effects persist for building height, and distances to green and water, especially for winter gas, indicating additional, unmodeled pathways. Partial dependence plots are used to assess the nature of the relationship. Sensitivity analyses for context size, model specifications, regularization, spatial autocorrelation, and sub-contexts are conducted, offering comparative and methodological insights. Overall, the study clarifies how urban form influences energy use, informing urban planning and energy policies.

title: Interpretable machine learning of urban noise levels from street-scale morphology and functionality
abstract: • Data-driven, non-causal framework links street morphology to urban noise. • Daytime in situ noise measurements capture street-scale spatial variability. • Street functional hierarchy dominates noise exposure across cities. • Interpretable ML reveals nonlinear effects and key urban design indicators. • Results support noise screening and planning in data-constrained cities. Urban noise exposure is shaped not only by traffic intensity but also by the spatial configuration and functional hierarchy of streets. Traditional prediction approaches, however, often prioritize traffic flow while underrepresenting the role of urban form. This study examines how street-scale morphological and functional characteristics are associated with environmental noise levels across four Chilean cities with contrasting urban structures. A total of 530 daytime in situ measurements of the equivalent continuous sound level L A e q were combined with 71 urban predictors derived from municipal records and open-source data within 150 m buffers around each sampling location. Three ensemble learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) were optimized using Bayesian hyperparameter search and evaluated under intra-city validation, achieving strong explanatory power ( R ² = 0.65–0.95) and high accuracy ( MAE ≈ 1.5–2.2 dBA). Cross-city evaluation using a leave-one-city-out scheme revealed moderate performance degradation when predicting unseen urban contexts, highlighting both the potential and limits of territorial transferability. Model interpretability analyses based on LightGBM gain, SHAP values, and LIME explanations consistently identified street functional hierarchy as the dominant indicator associated with urban noise exposure, followed by roadway capacity and land-use intensity. Spatial patterns revealed elevated noise levels (>65 dBA) along higher-order arterial corridors, while quieter conditions were typically associated with lower-category residential streets. Overall, the results show that interpretable machine learning provides a transparent, data-driven, and non-causal framework for linking urban form and function to street-level noise patterns, supporting noise screening and urban planning in data-constrained contexts.

verified_metadata.title: How natural–built environments shape spatiotemporal patterns of urban heat islands: Integrating water-gradient stratification and machine learning
verified_metadata.abstract: Urban heat islands (UHI) have intensified with urban expansion and climate warming. In waterfront cities, built environments (BE) have developed in close interaction with water-related natural environments (NE), yet the role of natural–built environments (NBE) in shaping UHI spatiotemporal patterns remains unclear. This study used Wuhan as a case city and classified the entire area into six waterfront gradients (L1–L6). The dataset included a multidimensional NBE index system and land surface temperatures (LST), serving as a key indicator for UHI from 2013 to 2023. At the system level, bivariate spatial autocorrelation and geographically and temporally weighted regression (GTWR) models were employed to elucidate the spatiotemporal interactions between NBE and UHI. At the factor level, Pearson correlation and machine learning models were combined to identify multi-gradient stratified responses of key drivers. Results showed a 3.60 % decline in NE, mainly in L1–L3, and a 14.21 % increase in BE, concentrated in L3–L4. UHI was strongest in L1–L2, with LST of 35.20 °C and 35.40 °C, while L6 exhibited lower LST (32.64 °C). LST’s standard deviation ellipses aligned with the Yangtze River, but centroid shifts and hotspot evolution diverged from NE. In L6, NE showed a mitigating effect on UHI (GTWR = −0.18), while in L4, BE showed strong positive reinforcement (GTWR = 0.70). Random forest–SHAP analysis further revealed strong spatiotemporal heterogeneity in marginal contributions of NBE factors to UHI. BE factors formed synergistic warming peaks in L1–L3 with cumulative amplification over time. In L4, compensatory effects between BE and NE became stronger. In inland L5–L6 gradients, NE showed stage-dependent UHI mitigation effects, with delayed gradient responses activated when ecological thresholds exceeded 0.5. These findings provide evidence for climate-resilient planning in waterfront cities and support SDGs 11 and 13.

verified_metadata.title: Applications and challenges of machine learning in urban thermal environment: A systematic review
verified_metadata.abstract: The synergistic pressure of urbanization and global warming requires us to develop powerful analytical tools to interpret the complex dynamic changes in the urban thermal environment (UTE). This study adopts the PRISMA system evaluation method. Through the core database and strict literature screening process, 493 studies that meet the inclusion criteria are screened from the 3299 literatures originally retrieved. The research systematically summarizes the application status and technical characteristics of machine learning (ML) algorithm in four major subject areas: UTE prediction and simulation, urban spatial morphology research, architectural morphology analysis, and urban thermal vulnerability and thermal comfort assessment. The research results show that supervised learning (SL) (especially random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM) and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)) dominates feature extraction and prediction tasks, while multi-source data such as remote sensing and land coverage are used as core inputs. Crucially, the field is undergoing a paradigm shift from a single predictive model to a comprehensive framework that integrates interpretability and optimization. Despite these advances, challenges persist in data quality, the opacity of the "black box" model, and cross-regional mobility. In order to solve these problems, this paper distills practical implementation suggestions from the aspects of computing resources, missing data processing, spatial cross-verification and uncertainty quantification, providing systematic theoretical reference and methodological guidance for researchers in the field of UTE, as well as resilient urban development, thermal risk management and sustainability.

verified_metadata.title: A Data Assimilation-Informed Deep Learning Framework for Transient Turbulent Urban Wind Field Prediction: Integrating Sparse High-Fidelity Data and Low-Resolution Simulations
verified_metadata.abstract: Rapid and accurate prediction of wind speed fields in urban environments is vital for understanding the urban climate, promoting urban sustainability, and disaster mitigation. However, progress in this field continues to face two significant limitations, namely the substantial computational demands of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods, and the inherent challenge of error accumulation in deep learning approaches. To address these issues, we propose a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based data assimilation model that serves as a CFD surrogate model, aiming to enhance computational efficiency while improving transient urban wind field prediction accuracy. By integrating a novel temporally enhanced hybrid U-Net architecture, the generator enables precise flow field pattern prediction. The discriminator leverages sparse high-precision data for dynamic assimilation and correction to improve the stability and accuracy of long-term predictions. The results of our experiments across multiple scenarios show that our model outperforms CFD numerical simulation methods by two orders of magnitude in efficiency, reduces the MAE and MSE by 29.2% and 38.6% respectively compared with CFD-URANS simulations, and significantly enhances turbulent flow characteristic reconstruction, thus providing a highly efficient data assimilation framework for simulating wind speed fields in urban environments.

verified_metadata.title: Hybrid deep reinforcement learning for optimizing electric vehicle charging station placement: Multi agent-based simulations using real-world data
verified_metadata.abstract: The strategic placement of electric vehicle (EV) charging stations is essential to accelerate EV adoption and ensure sustainable urban mobility. Existing research often proposes theoretical solutions that overlook practical constraints that limit their practical impact. To bridge this gap between theory and practice, in this study we propose a new hybrid deep reinforcement learning (HDRL) framework that incorporates critical real-world operational and financial constraints to guide actionable decision-making. Our approach uses a graph neural network (GNN) to represent the road network, distances, and accessibility score data of the city in the form of a spatial graph, effectively capturing the complex interdependencies between potential station locations. This graphical representation facilitates the learning of a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent, which is trained to determine the optimal set of locations that maximizes station accessibility while respecting constraints. A key part of our analysis includes a comparative evaluation of the performance and cost–benefit of two common charging technologies, 22 kW and 50 kW chargers, to determine the optimal technology for the proposed infrastructure plan. In addition, we determine the ideal number of chargers for each station, which is a crucial variable that is often ignored or fixed. To ensure robustness, the results obtained are simulated in the simulation of urban mobility (SUMO) environment using real data, generating realistic usage statistics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed HDRL framework significantly outperforms traditional placement strategies when evaluated based on key metrics including average user wait times, budget allocation efficiency, charger utilization rates, and overall network accessibility. These findings offer a flexible and practical tool for reducing infrastructure investment risks and accelerating the transition to electric mobility.

verified_metadata.title: Exposure-Aware commuting: Geo-AI–Driven route optimization to reduce NO2 in urban road networks
verified_metadata.abstract: Air pollution exposure during daily commuting poses significant health risks, yet most route-planning studies focus on PM₂.₅ and rely on coarse spatial interpolation methods. This study advances exposure-aware mobility by developing a high-resolution geospatial artificial intelligence (Geo-AI) framework for Kaohsiung City, Taiwan. This framework models nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), a traffic-related pollutant with sharp spatial gradients, and integrates it into an optimized route-planning system. A Light Gradient Boosting Machine Regression (LGBMR) model was trained on continuous monitoring data from December 2021 to February 2024. The model achieved robust predictive performance (R² = 0.87), enabling reliable estimates of pollutant concentrations at the street segment scale. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis revealed that chemical-industry density, waste-treatment facility density, and road network density were among the most influential predictors of elevated NO₂. By combining 10 × 10 m NO₂ concentration data from the model and a detailed road network database, we simulated 3000 randomized commuting routes and compared distance-optimized and exposure-optimized routing scenarios. On average, low-exposure routing reduced NO₂ exposure by 2.04%, while 259 routes achieved reductions of over 5%. In some cases, the reduction reached 39.70%. A representative 365-day commuting simulation was conducted for the entire year of 2024. It projected an annual cumulative reduction in exposure of 9.02 × 10⁵ ppb·s for a typical commuter using optimized routes. These results underscore the feasibility and public health potential of integrating high-resolution pollutant mapping with route optimization, enabling personalized, exposure-conscious mobility. It offers a scalable pathway for urban planners and policymakers to mitigate long-term health risks, especially in densely populated Asian cities with high motor vehicle use.

verified_metadata.title: Hazard-responsive digital twin for weather-driven urban resilience and affordability
verified_metadata.abstract: Compounding weather hazards, such as wildfire-induced outages and urban heatwaves, challenge the reliability, affordability, and safety of urban services. We present a Hazard-Responsive Digital Twin (H-RDT) that combines physics-informed neural network modeling, multimodal data fusion, affiliation learning, and affordability-aware risk analytics for urban-scale response. In a screening-level synthetic district with diverse building archetypes and populations, a simulated wildfire–outage–heatwave cascade shows that H-RDT maintains stable indoor temperature predictions (∼31–33 °C peaks) under partial sensor loss, while reproducing outage-driven surges and recovery. The reinforcement learning based fusion module adaptively reweights IoT, UAV, and satellite inputs to sustain spatiotemporal coverage, and the affordability-adjusted mapping isolates high-vulnerability clusters such as schools, clinics, low-income housing. Prospective interventions, i.e., preemptive cooling-center activation and microgrid sharing, reduce population-weighted thermal risk by 11–13%, shrink the 95th-percentile (tail) risk by 7–17%, and cut overheating hours by up to 9%. Beyond this synthetic demonstration, the framework establishes a transferable pathway for real-city implementation by linking hazard modeling, reliability-focused analytics, and decision intelligence for resilience planning.

verified_metadata.title: Artificial intelligence enhanced workflow for noise conscious urban design in high density cities
verified_metadata.abstract: Acoustic comfort becomes critical for health and the quality of life in dense metropolises, yet responses from urban planning and design are limited. Existing noise mitigation relies on regulations of urban density, street dimensions, or post-hoc diagnosis at project level, while advanced simulations are computationally intensive and not ready to be integrated into planning and design process. This study introduces a novel workflow to optimize building configurations under site constraints with the objective of reducing traffic noise exposure. The workflow employs a neural network model trained using a 3D urban noise dataset generated using an empirically validated, state-of-the-art simulation. The model was then coupled with a parametric building form generator and an evolutionary algorithm to iteratively identify optimal building configurations. The workflow was tested with a high-rise mixed-use development in Hong Kong, where results indicated reductions of average traffic noise exposure of up to 1.54 dB compared to a baseline design, and 3.53 dB compared with the least effective configuration. These noise reductions resulted from optimized building massing and spatial configurations that balance sound energy shielded by buildings with that reflected in street canyons. Analysis using gradient boosting regression and SHapley Additive exPlanations further revealed the non-linear relationships between noise exposure and parameters such as position-dependent building volume and average building height-to-distance ratio, suggesting the current noise regulations may be insufficient. The proposed workflow demonstrates potentials to inform urban planning and design practices by incorporating traffic noise exposure mitigation as a design objective.

title: Hemispheric-Scale assessment of urban morphology effects on NO₂ dynamics via LSTM-Based counterfactuals and structural equation modeling
abstract: Understanding how urban morphology influences air pollution during unexpected events such as COVID-19 lockdowns is essential for sustainable urban planning. However, existing studies often lack sufficient impact diversity analysis in urban form and environmental context. To address this gap, we developed an integrated analytical framework by synergizing long short-term memory (LSTM)-based counterfactual predictions with structural equation modeling (SEM). Specifically, lockdown-induced daily ground-based NO₂ variations across North America, Europe and East Asia were first quantified. Subsequently, SEM was used to evaluate how urban forms drive the variations based on 12 indicators of building and road characteristics. Results show that the LSTM model achieved superior performance in NO₂ prediction (R 2 = 0.9), with greater lockdown-induced reductions in Asia, followed by Europe and North America. SEM revealed the joint effects of building and road indicators on NO₂ changes, where floor area ratio (FAR) and area coverage ratio (ACR) as the most influential building indicators, while road intersection density (RID) and traffic point density (TPD) are the dominant road indicators. Furthermore, the impacts of urban forms show significant regional heterogeneity. NO 2 reductions in coastal, high-GDP, and high-population cities were primarily driven by decreased traffic activity. In contrast, inland, low-GDP, and low-population cities were more limited by urban form and dispersion capacity. These research results highlight the importance of developing urban design and emission reduction strategies for specific environments to improve air quality and enhance urban resilience in the post-epidemic era.

title: A scalable, automatic, and evolutionary algorithm for calibrating urban building energy models
abstract: • Scalable EA CMA-ES/HDE for UBEM calibration at building and block scale • Large-scale application of optimisation-based calibration to 200 buildings • Representative user-behaviour in archetype-based UBEMs The national building renovation plan, which has been established under the newly approved Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EU 2024/1275), can be effectively supported by combining Urban Building Energy Modelling (UBEM) with building archetyping. However, due to inaccessible, unavailable, and inaccurate city-wide building energy consumption data—and the high computational cost of iteratively running large-scale energy models—most UBEM applications remain unvalidated and uncalibrated. This work presents a novel methodology aimed at improving the credibility, transparency, and reliability of national building renovation plans. Specifically, it introduces an automatic calibration procedure for archetype-based UBEMs, using a scalable optimisation algorithm CMA-ES/HDE, which combines the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy with Hybrid Differential Evolution techniques. Depending on the spatial resolution of the available energy consumption data, the procedure was applied both at the single-building and aggregated multi-building scales within the CitySim environment. The methodology was tested on approximately 200 buildings in the municipality of Monthey (Switzerland). Calibration was achieved by minimising the coefficient of variation of the root-mean-square error, CV(RMSE) , between predicted and observed daily space heating and domestic hot water demands. Using a CV(RMSE) threshold of 25 %, calibration was successful in 43 % of cases at the individual building level; the resulting calibrated parameter ranges were then used to guide the subsequent multi-building calibration. While the methodology does not incorporate the engineering expertise typically applied in manual calibration, it remains a practical and scalable approach for large-scale UBEM calibration, providing valuable insights for future applications.

title: From simulation to surrogates: optimizing green roofs for sustainable urban performance
abstract: Green roofs (GRs) constitute a key nature-based solution for mitigating the adverse effects of urbanization, including heat accumulation, stormwater runoff, and biodiversity loss. Over the past two decades, research has progressed from empirical evaluations of GR performance toward computational frameworks that optimize their multifunctional behavior. This review systematically synthesizes and critically examines Multi-Objective Optimization methodologies applied to GR systems, with emphasis on Simulation-Based Optimization and Surrogate-Assisted Optimization approaches that enable efficient exploration of complex, high-dimensional, and multi-criteria design spaces. An extensive review of the available research identified 21 studies that explicitly applied optimization methodologies to GR systems, are analyzed according to their optimization objectives, methodological configurations, and spatial scale of application. Although recent advances have improved the analytical rigor of GR research, most optimization-oriented studies remain fragmented, prioritizing a limited subset of objectives—most frequently building energy performance and stormwater management. Thermal comfort and microclimate regulation are often treated as secondary objectives or embedded within energy- or spatial-cooling metrics, and cross-domain feedback between thermal, hydrological, and ecological processes remains insufficiently explored. A systematic synthesis of reviewed optimization frameworks reveals that integration between physical simulations and data-driven surrogates is often modular rather than fully coupled. Simulation engines and surrogate models are predominantly linked through sequential or hierarchical workflows rather than dynamic co-simulation, and few frameworks incorporate uncertainty quantification, life-cycle metrics, or adaptive vegetation dynamics. Nature, however, functions synthetically—through continuous interactions among thermal, hydrological, and ecological processes. GRs embody this principle, transforming inert surfaces into living systems that improve energy efficiency, water regulation, and carbon sequestration while enhancing urban well-being. Future optimization frameworks must therefore emulate this natural integrative logic through coupled multi-physics and data-driven modeling, positioning GRs as adaptive mediators within the urban energy–water–ecology continuum.

verified_metadata.title: An AI-driven MABM–BIM–DL framework for energy consumption prediction in three representative types of urban public buildings in Wuhan
verified_metadata.abstract: Accurate prediction of energy consumption in urban public buildings is essential for city planning and sustainable development, yet remains challenging when indoor layouts and occupant behaviors differ across building types. Taking Wuhan as the study context, this work proposes an AI-driven framework for public-building energy prediction that integrates multi-building agent-based modeling (MABM), building information modeling (BIM), and deep learning (DL) to forecast energy use in hospitals, shopping malls and office buildings. An MABM-BIM model is first developed and then calibrated and validated against one year of measured data from the three building types. The model explicitly represents the coupled processes among indoor layout, occupant behavior and energy use, and generates synthetic energy time series that are both behaviorally plausible and consistent with widely used calibration criteria. On this basis, four deep learning predictors (DNN, RNN, LSTM and Transformer) are trained on a combination of simulated and measured data and are benchmarked against a representative baseline model from the literature. Across the three building types, the proposed AI models increase R2 by 12.9%–14.0% and Accuracy by 12.2%–13.0%, while reducing MSE, MAE and MAAPE. The Transformer delivers the best overall performance, highlighting the advantage of attention-based architectures for learning long-horizon temporal dependencies and cross-feature interactions. The trained predictors can be embedded as BIM-linked modules to support rapid energy estimation in planning and conceptual design, thus enabling data-driven scheme screening and sustainability-oriented decision-making for public buildings in hot-summer and cold-winter climatic regions.

verified_metadata.title: Attributing the urban heat island effect to urban land use patterns with integrated machine learning and GeoShapley method
verified_metadata.abstract: Urban land-use patterns are fundamentally associated with the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. However, conventional models struggle to capture the complex non-linear associations and spatial heterogeneity between land layouts and Land Surface Temperature (LST). This study characterizes these associations using high-resolution land-use data and a spatially interpretable framework integrating machine learning with the GeoShapley method. To ensure methodological robustness, a Spatial Block Cross-Validation (SBCV) strategy was implemented. Layout features were quantified across four dimensions: coverage, connectivity, complexity, and aggregation. Key findings indicate:(1) After decoupling the background thermal effects of geographic location, green space and agricultural land are identified as the optimal land types for heat mitigation, while industrial land is the primary contributor to UHI intensification. In terms of land layout, coverage and connectivity exert significantly greater influence on the thermal environment than aggregation and complexity. (2) Residential and green space coverage exhibit monotonic associations with the UHI effect. In contrast, agricultural and industrial coverage demonstrate pronounced threshold effects, where their impacts stabilize after reaching specific levels.(3) The UHI attribution of land use displays significant spatial heterogeneity, most prominently in green space coverage, whose cooling efficiency is notably attenuated in high-density built-up areas.(4) The impacts of different land-use combinations on the UHI effect vary significantly, with some combinations generating synergistic effects while others exhibit spatial substitution. By identifying dominant land types and sensitive layout intervals, this study deepens the understanding of urban climate mechanisms and provides a scientific basis for formulating precise thermal environment management strategies.

verified_metadata.title: Unraveling the coupling-driven patterns of urban carbon emissions and urban heat islands: An LCZ-based interpretable machine learning approach
verified_metadata.abstract: The coupling of Urban Carbon Emissions (UCE) and Urban Heat Islands (UHI) poses a critical challenge to sustainable urban development. While their static correlation is widely recognized, the mechanisms underlying their dynamic synchrony remain poorly understood. Furthermore, traditional urban morphological indicators are often limited in identifying priority intervention areas and may fail to capture the heterogeneity driven by diverse climatic and economic backgrounds. To address this, this study adopted the Local Climate Zone (LCZ) framework as a standardized physical descriptor to unravel UCE–UHI coupling patterns. Based on data from 2714 counties in China, we developed an XGBoost-TPE model combined with SHAP to facilitate mechanistic insights. Our key findings were as follows: (1) UCE and UHI in Chinese counties from 2015 to 2021 exhibited a significant global positive correlation (Moran’s I: 0.203–0.212, p-value < 0.01), but showed asynchronous dynamic changes in the northwest and western regions. (2) The LCZ-based model demonstrated high predictive consistency across all clusters (R2 of cross-validation > 0.85). (3) The key drivers of UCE and UHI exhibited heterogeneity: built-type LCZs appeared to be more critical for UCE, while natural-type LCZs tended to exert a more pronounced influence on UHI. (4) LCZs’ effects varied significantly with climatic backgrounds, with different directions, magnitudes, and transition thresholds (LCZs 2–3: 0.2%–6.9%, LCZs 4–6: 1.3%–20.5%, LCZs 7–10: 0.8%–13.9%, LCZs E-F: 1.2%–1.3%). (5) Synergistic, antagonistic, and complex phase-based compound interactions between LCZs were identified. By linking urban morphological characteristics with environmental responses, this study highlights the analytical potential of the LCZ framework for diagnosing UCE–UHI coupling dynamics. The results provide a quantitative, evidence-informed basis to support context-sensitive urban planning and targeted mitigation strategies.

verified_metadata.title: Unraveling the impacts of multidimensional urban influencing factors on daytime and nighttime thermal environments across urban functional zones using SDGSAT-1 data and XGBoost-GeoShapley analysis
verified_metadata.abstract: Although numerous researches have explored how urban influencing factors influences land surface temperature (LST), comparatively limited attention has been given to analyses based on urban functional zones (UFZs), especially those that investigate and contrast the driving mechanisms between daytime and nighttime conditions. Furthermore, numerous studies have analyzed this driving mechanism using interpretable machine learning methods that typically rely on the standard SHAP framework, yet this approach overlooks the inherent spatial dependency. In our study, high-resolution daytime and nighttime thermal infrared data from SDGSAT-1 were integrated with multi-source urban datasets for Fuzhou, China. An interpretable integrated XGBoost-GeoShapley framework was applied to comprehensively investigate the determinants of LST during summer daytime and nighttime among six predominant UFZs. The results reveal a fundamental daytime and nighttime shift in thermal drivers: built-environment indices dictate daytime sensible heat accumulation, whereas ecological factors dominate nocturnal latent heat cooling. Simultaneously building density acts as a severe daytime warmer but transitions to a relative nocturnal cooler in dense commercial cores due to the urban canyon mutual shading effect. Furthermore, ecological cooling demonstrates a biological threshold. Crucially, GeoShapley analysis uncovers that spatial interaction effects are substantially stronger at night, accounting for 38.2% of the integrated zone, with residential zones reaching 33.6%. This research establishes a spatially explicit analytical framework to unravel the multifactorial influences shaping the urban thermal environment and delivers scientific evidence that supports the development of spatially and temporally adaptive strategies for urban heat mitigation and planning.

verified_metadata.title: Enhancing thermal resilience of heat–cold island networks in lake-ring urban agglomerations using machine learning and multi-scenario simulations
verified_metadata.abstract: Under rapid urbanization and climate warming, urban heat island (UHI) effects in lake-ring urban agglomerations have intensified. Prior studies often emphasize single patches or local scales, obscuring regional heat–cold connectivity and limiting network-based resilience planning under future scenarios. This study integrates morphological spatial pattern analysis (MSPA) with circuit theory to construct a heat–cold island (HCI) composite network comprising sources, corridors, and nodes. In this framework, machine learning characterizes nonlinear thermal-connectivity resistance, while the patch-generating land-use simulation (PLUS) model simulates HCI network reorganization under multiple 2030 scenarios. A land surface temperature (LST)-derived surface thermal structural resilience framework was then developed to link historical and future network changes. Evidence from the Taihu Lake urban agglomeration indicates that from 2000 to 2020, heat island (HI) sources expanded rapidly across the eastern lakeside built-up area, with marked increases in corridors and nodes. In contrast, cold island (CI) networks became increasingly fragmented. HCI composite nodes shifted from the Taihu Lake shoreline toward the western ecological transition zone. By 2030, SSP585 formed a strong heat-connectivity network, and cooling connectivity pathways were nearly lost. Under SSP119, barriers to cold-source connectivity were reduced, and CI corridors increased. The surface thermal structural resilience improvement index (TR) showed strong structural dependence, remaining negative historically and declining further under SSP245 and SSP585. By contrast, SSP119 increased TR to −0.134 through cooling-corridor recovery and key-node reorganization, approaching a more balanced network structure. This study reframes LST-based surface thermal structural resilience from a whole-network HCI perspective and provides guidance for climate-adaptive spatial planning.

title: Data-driven risk assessment of climate-related failures in railway infrastructure
abstract: Climate-related failures pose increasing risks to railway operation and maintenance, requiring robust assessments to support effective resilience planning. Accordingly, this study presents a comprehensive risk assessment to identify, quantify, and prioritize climate-related failure modes (CRFMs). CRFMs were identified through text mining of 15-year corrective maintenance records across all five Swedish railway regions. A probabilistic model was then developed to analyze the risk of identified CRFMs, considering both operational and maintenance costs. Risk distributions were derived using Monte Carlo simulation and summarized by Expected Value of Risk (EVoR) and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR 0.90 ). As a result, 14 CRFMs were identified, accounting for 47% of all failure records. Their annual trend and seasonal distribution align well with periods of increased extreme weather events and dominant seasonal climate hazards. Furthermore, clustering the regional profile of CRFMs reveals regional similarity. The CRFMs were then prioritized, showing that 4 modes (i.e., Track deformation, Snow and ice, Buckling, and Rail breakage/crack) account for 73% of total CVaR 0.90 . The amplification of total risk in the tail indicates a 74% higher cost burden under extreme conditions. Finally, regional climate vulnerability was assessed using risk metrics normalized by track length and traffic density.

verified_metadata.title: Deciphering the impacts of urban gray–green spaces on seasonal diurnal land surface temperature in a valley-basin city via explainable machine learning
verified_metadata.abstract: The Urban Heat Island effect poses a major challenge to sustainable development, and understanding its driving factors is crucial for improving the urban thermal environment. The nonlinear effects of urban gray–green spaces on Land Surface Temperature (LST) under valley-basin conditions remain systematically underexplored. This study investigates Changsha, a typical valley-basin city, by integrating Morphological Spatial Pattern Analysis with landscape metrics to construct a comprehensive gray–green spaces framework. Using explainable machine learning (CatBoost-SHAP), we quantify the nonlinear and interactive effects of eight composite indicators on seasonal diurnal LST. Results show: (1) Gray space indicators contribute 51.6–59.2% to daytime LST across spring, summer, and winter, with BMSF as the dominant positive driver; green space indicators contribute 57.5–65.2% to nighttime LST, led by GACI and GMSF. (2) Threshold effects are evident: BMSF warming saturates beyond +0.5 SD, while GCI cooling diminishes after +0.5 SD, with marginal returns dropping from 0.25 °C per unit to near zero. GACI shows a unique positive effect (+0.3 °C) on winter nights. (3) Interactions reveal synergistic heating (BMSF×BCI > 0.25 SHAP), synergistic cooling (GMSF×GCI <−0.4 SHAP), and asymmetric buffering where high GMSF reduces BMSF thermal load by up to 0.6 SHAP. This study underscores gray–green interplay as a key driver of urban thermal dynamics in valley-basin cities, revealing quantifiable nonlinear balances. Based on these findings, we propose a regulatory strategy integrating spatiotemporal control, synergistic optimization, and topographic adaptation.

verified_metadata.title: Identifying CO2 emission reduction strategies tailored to different building types by integrating multi-scale factors via deep learning
verified_metadata.abstract: Reducing carbon emissions in the building sector is a critical challenge for urban decarbonization. Buildings differ substantially in their functions, usage intensities, and operational characteristics, which require emission reduction strategies tailored to different building types. However, previous studies have been limited in their examination of how building-level characteristics and the surrounding urban environments jointly influence CO2 emissions across different building types. Therefore, this study proposes an artificial intelligence-based analytical framework that integrates building-level characteristics with urban environmental factors to assess their effects on CO2 emissions across different building types. This framework captures non-linear relationships between the multi-scale factors and CO2 emissions and assesses their effects using model interpretation techniques, simulating changes from current states. The findings of this study indicate that increasing floor area ratio (FAR) generally reduces CO2 emissions, whereas emissions increase in public buildings when the FAR is increased by 140% relative to its current level. Increasing south-facing building surface area showed the potential to substantially reduce emissions in low-rise residential and public buildings. Furthermore, the increased green area ratio (GAR) effectively mitigated emissions in residential buildings, while exhibiting a rebound effect in commercial buildings when increased by 12%. These findings highlight the importance of building-type-specific and threshold-based strategies for effective urban building decarbonization. Moreover, this framework provides quantitative evidence for developing building-type-specific regulatory standards and design guidelines, supporting more targeted and effective urban building decarbonization.

verified_metadata.title: A comparative assessment of sampling strategies for tree-based machine learning models in urban flood susceptibility prediction with imbalanced data
verified_metadata.abstract: Flood susceptibility mapping identifies flood-prone areas, providing scientific support for flood prevention planning and resilient infrastructure. However, the accuracy of machine learning models in flood susceptibility mapping is compromised by imbalanced data. Moreover, systematic comparative assessments of sampling strategies for tree-based models in urban flood susceptibility prediction are lacking, and the intricate nonlinear correlations between flood susceptibility and its underlying drivers remain insufficiently explored. This study developed a novel framework that systematically investigates the effect of sampling methods and non-flooding samples ratios on tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) in urban flood susceptibility prediction in Beijing, China, and places a dual emphasis on predictive performance and model interpretability via Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) analyses to interpret the key drivers. Results show that models using one-class support vector machine (OC SVM) method (Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) ≥ 0.92) consistently outperformed those using random sampling at 1:3 and 1:5 ratios. Specifically, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model with OC SVM at a 1:3 ratio attained the highest AUC value (0.938) and Geometric Mean (G-mean) (0.845) across all sampling methods and ratios, and exhibited a more balanced and rational spatial pattern in flood susceptibility prediction. The top four factors contributing to flood susceptibility were Gross Domestic Product (GDP) level (28.04%), mean building height (15.96%), distance to roads (15.31%), and Digital Elevation Model (DEM) (9.67%). PDP analysis revealed urban flood susceptibility initially increases significantly with GDP, and then declines and stabilizes after a critical point. A strong near-linear positive relationship was evident between building height and flood susceptibility. Flood susceptibility significantly decreases as distance to roads increased and eventually stabilizes. This study provides empirical evidence and methodological guidance for selecting sampling strategies in applying machine learning models for urban flood susceptibility prediction.

title: Toward interpretable urban spatial layout generation: Encoding domain knowledge into graph neural networks
abstract: While deep neural networks advance urban spatial layout (USL) generation, the uninterpretable nature restricts their practical application in human-value-aligned planning scenarios. This study presents the Hierarchical Causal Graph Neural Network with Domain Knowledge Constraints (HCGNN-DKC). This is a neuro-symbolic model that internalises the ontology and expert priors from the planning domain into the information delivery mechanism, while further regularising the model’s predictive scope through logical rules. Evaluations indicate that HCGNN-DKC significantly outperforms baseline models in performance (average accuracy of 85.2%, recall of 74.1%, MSE of 0.523) and generalisability. Crucially, rule-violation test results and real-world applications prove that the embedded logical rules serve as a safety guardrail, effectively mitigating physical violations. Furthermore, whilst adhering to prior knowledge, the model exhibits an autonomous knowledge discovery capability that transcends expert presets. The semantic proximity shown by our framework provides a vital bridge between planning semantics and spatial modelling, establishing an interpretable and intelligent knowledge-based planning support systems.

verified_metadata.title: Automated urban energy assessment: From thermal flyover to AI-driven retrofit prioritization for sustainable cities
verified_metadata.abstract: Cities urgently need scalable methods to assess building energy performance for retrofit prioritization, yet current approaches are costly and slow for comprehensive urban energy planning. We present an automated pipeline that transforms thermal flyovers into actionable energy assessments using AI-driven analysis. Our approach segments mid-wave infrared orthomosaics into building patches using an unsupervised multi-modal pipeline (Thermal-SAM), extracts physically interpretable ring and context features, and benchmarks energy-use intensity (EUI) derived from aggregated EPC records. We exclude implausible EUI records above 1000 kWh/m2/yr from primary model-performance evaluation. On this screened dataset (n=1190), leakage-free non-thermal covariates achieve RMSE = 26.84 and MAE = 16.13 kWh/m2/yr, within the range reported by recent EPC-based prediction studies. An EPC-full upper-bound model that retains energy-consumption proxies achieves lower error (RMSE = 9.36, MAE = 1.31 kWh/m2/yr), but this reflects feature–target proximity rather than independent prediction. Thermal features are therefore not presented as routine direct EUI predictors. Instead, the excluded high-EUI tail is treated as a diagnostic anomaly set: in the unfiltered diagnostic analysis, thermal features help rank the largest thermal–EPC discrepancies (AUC = 0.779, 95% CI 0.774–0.784, 100 seeds), while this signal collapses after the implausible records are removed. These findings reposition thermal flyovers as a scalable tool for triaging buildings with unusually high or inconsistent EPC-derived energy use, while highlighting the limitations of single-pass thermal data for accurate EUI regression. Reproducible code (available upon request) supports rapid, citywide screening and targeted follow-up audits.

title: Causal machine learning uncovers thresholds and seasonal reversal in landscape-meteorology-driven urban Heat-PM₂.₅ coupling
abstract: In the context of rapid urbanization, the mutual amplification between the urban heat island (UHI) effect and air pollution has emerged as a severe composite environmental challenge. Most existing studies focus on the linear driving mechanisms of individual environmental issues, leaving a systematic understanding of their nonlinear interactions, seasonal dynamics, and causal pathways largely unexplored. To address this gap, this study focuses on the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration in China as a case study. It bridges interpretable machine learning (XGBoost-SHAP) with structural causal modeling (SCM) to systematically quantify the nonlinear impacts and causal mechanisms of blue-green space (BGS) patterns and meteorological factors on land surface temperature (LST) and PM 2.5 concentrations. The results indicate that: (1) LST drivers exhibit a pronounced seasonal shift-BGS coverage dominates in summer, whereas meteorological factors prevail in winter-whereas PM 2.5 is consistently governed by wind speed across seasons; (2) key drivers exhibit threshold effects (e.g., in this study, 40-42% vegetation coverage for LST, 79-80% water aggregation for PM 2.5 ), beyond which they act as “effect-switching thresholds” that reverse the influence of other factors and form a nonlinear interaction network; and (3) SCM reveals the dual causal pathways through which BGS patterns influence the environment-via direct cooling and indirect modulation of wind fields-and quantitatively verifies the stable positive causal effect of PM 2.5 on LST, clarifying the pathway of “pollution exacerbating warming”. In summary, this study uncovers the nonlinear, threshold-dependent characteristics of the UHI-pollution complex system and elucidates their synergistic intensification from a causal perspective, providing a quantitative basis for seasonally adaptive strategies to synergistically mitigate urban heat and pollution.

verified_metadata.title: Enhancing interdependent infrastructure systems resilience in post-disaster recovery: A social-technical approach based on reinforcement learning
verified_metadata.abstract: A social-technical approach integrating the Infrastructure Hetero-functional Graph (IHFG) and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is proposed for the collaborative recovery of post-disaster multi-infrastructure systems. A "physical entity–functional node–service process" mapping mechanism is established to explicitly characterize complex system interdependencies. Furthermore, a reward mechanism driven by hierarchical resident needs is integrated to facilitate service-oriented recovery within highly dynamic and complex environments. In a case study of a coupled transportation-power-gas-water network in Jingdezhen, optimal repair strategies under multi-hazard scenarios were explored. The results show that IHFG-MARL with dynamic weights can generate system-level recovery strategies that account for complex interdependencies and achieve relatively robust resilience improvement under different disaster conditions. In rainfall-driven scenarios, the proposed method and the genetic algorithm both show strong performance, whereas the advantage of IHFG-MARL with dynamic weights becomes more evident under the full-damage stress-test scenario. This indicates that the proposed method has stronger strategic adaptability in complex interdependent networks and under high-intensity disturbances. In addition, the embedded dynamic demand mechanism enables the recovery process to prioritize residents’ basic survival needs and gradually shift toward broader functional service needs as recovery progresses, thereby forming recovery pathways consistent with the hierarchical evolution of residents’ needs.

title: Urban airflow field prediction using sparse sensors: A hybrid data-driven approach with reduced-order modeling
abstract: Urban airflow field modeling can provide cities with monitoring solutions to enhance pedestrian/cyclists comfort, improve air quality, and enhance urban wind energy generation yield. In addition, it could support a safe and efficient deployment of urban air mobility (UAM) supporting the next generation of faster and more sustainable means of urban transport reducing the congestion and traffic. However, real-time wind monitoring across urban areas remains a significant challenge due to spatial and temporal variations and uncertainties. This study presents an integrated framework that serves as a surrogate model for the real-time reconstruction and prediction of wind velocity fields around a simplified urban building configuration. The approach relies exclusively on online sensor measurements and employs reduced-order modeling techniques for dimensionality reduction, thereby improving computational efficiency. The offline development of the model integrates three principal components: (1) a bidirectional long short-term memory (BILSTM) network trained on airflow sensor data to capture temporal dynamics, (2) a sparsity-promoting dynamic mode decomposition (SP-DMD) for extracting dominant spatial modes of airflow, and (3) a multi-task learning (MTL) network to map sensor signals. The proposed framework was assessed against high-fidelity CFD simulations of wind flow around a high-rise urban building. The results indicate that the proposed three-stage method reliably reconstructs accurate urban airflow fields in real time under varying levels of sensor noise, and demonstrate its feasibility for sparse-sensor reconstruction under the tested sensor-placement configurations. Moreover, these findings demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly reduce operational/computational costs and shows strong potential as a surrogate tool for next-generation of urban airflow monitoring.

verified_metadata.title: Revealing the diurnal drivers of land surface temperature using artificial neural network models: A case study in Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan metropolitan area, China
verified_metadata.abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified the urban heat island (UHI) effect, highlighting the need to better understand the factors associated with land surface temperature (LST) in order to improve local thermal environments. Although previous studies have shown that urbanization and environmental conditions can significantly influence LST, their relative importance, nonlinear relationships, and differences between daytime and nighttime remain insufficiently understood. The Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan (CZT) metropolitan area, one of China’s first national pilot zones for building a resource-efficient and environment-friendly society, is a representative metropolitan region characterized by a compact polycentric structure and pronounced natural-urban spatial heterogeneity. Using artificial neural network models and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), this study identifies the relative importance and nonlinear associations of multiple spatial and environmental factors with daytime and nighttime LST. This analysis is data-driven, and the physical mechanisms discussed in this study are intended only as plausible interpretations of the observed patterns rather than as directly tested processes. The results show that: (1) Elevation had the strongest association with both daytime and nighttime LST, followed by indicators of human activity intensity; (2) water bodies and densely vegetated areas exhibited clear cooling effects during the daytime, whereas water bodies showed relatively higher LST at night, shifting from daytime cold spots to nighttime hot spots; (3) all factors exhibited nonlinear associations with LST, and marginal effect curves revealed critical ranges and inflection points for daytime and nighttime LST variations; and (4) nonlinear statistical approaches are useful for quantitatively characterizing the complex relationships between LST and multiple spatial-environmental factors at the metropolitan scale. These findings provide refined and differentiated decision support for urban heat mitigation and spatial planning.

verified_metadata.title: Prioritizing ‘greenable areas’ for urban heat relief by integrating heat risk, cooling potential, and welfare equity: A data-driven framework with a case study of Nanjing, China
verified_metadata.abstract: Urban heat risk is intensifying in compact, high-density cities where opportunities for new green space are limited. Existing prioritization studies often identify where cooling is needed, but less often ask whether greening is feasible or where it would yield the largest marginal benefit. This study introduces greenable areas, defined as residual urban spaces that can be converted to vegetation within dense built-up fabrics. We develop a decision-support workflow that identifies these spaces, assesses heat risk, predicts scenario-based LST cooling with a machine-learning model, and estimates welfare gains in population-weighted green-space accessibility, with all outputs aggregated to street blocks. A case study in the main urban area of Nanjing, China shows how the framework can produce priority maps for feasible infill greening under limited land resources. By linking need, feasibility, cooling potential, and welfare equity, the study provides a replicable screening approach for urban heat adaptation in space-constrained environments.

title: Impact of natural and artificial cover on LST in cities, with a focus on comparison of single- and multi-ring buffers
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) is a representative indicator for predicting urban heat island. The single-buffer approach, which has been used to analyze the relationship between LST and explanatory variables, cannot capture the effects of both the distance of independent variables and the area of land cover included within the buffer zone. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the relationship between LST and natural and artificial land cover in urban regions, using a multi-ring buffer model to refine independent variables in 50-m increments, by land cover type. Four tree-based machine learning models—Random Forest, LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost—were compared. XGBoost exhibited the highest performance, with R² range of 0.88–0.98 across 50–500-m intervals. LST prediction analysis was effective up to 350 m. Further, the significant spatial range of variables shifted with 50-m intervals, enabling a more granular analysis of the significant spatial range of independent variables. The restoration simulation showed that greening efforts on the Western Arterial Road and Jemulpo Tunnel reduced LST within an approximate range of 150 m. These findings provide crucial scientific evidence for determining the placement of urban parks and formulating urban planning and management strategies aimed at optimizing LST reduction in urban environments.

verified_metadata.title: Strategic and equitable allocation of electric vehicle fast charging stations using geospatial-aware multi-objective deep reinforcement learning
verified_metadata.abstract: Public fast charging infrastructure is becoming an essential component of sustainable urban mobility as cities transition toward low-carbon transportation (e.g., Electric Vehicles (EVs)). However, suboptimal deployment can exacerbate spatial disparities in service accessibility, limit the practical benefits of EV adoption, and create localized stress on urban distribution grids. Despite recent advances in the allocation and placement of electric vehicle fast charging stations (FCSs), existing decision-support approaches remain limited in their ability to coordinate multiple objectives across large, spatially heterogeneous urban systems. This study thus proposes a multi-objective sequential decision-making model for the placement and sizing of FCS, integrated with solar power supply, across large and complex urban environments. By integrating a federated learning-based multi-objective deep reinforcement learning (FLMODRL) framework with geospatial analysis, the proposed model identifies EVFCS sites through a global policy that aggregates locally learned policies to achieve balanced performance across environmental, economic, and urbanity objectives. The proposed FLMORL model shows it capability to determine both the optimal placement and capacity of FCS by outperforming single-agent weight-summed reward scalarization deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Specifically, the model identifies 520 fast charging stations in Chicago that exceed a high reward threshold (e.g., >10), indicating locations that simultaneously satisfy all objectives. In addition, the proposed deployment scenario suggests the potential of the learned spatial allocation strategy to improve population-weighted accessibility across income groups in Chicago. Overall, the results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in supporting strategic and accessibility-aware FCS allocation across the urban area, contributing to more sustainable and resilient charging infrastructure planning.

title: From physical surfaces to human-centric heat stress: LST and UTCI heat mapping reveals nonlinear effects of urban morphology
abstract: Heat exposure connects the built environment and public health, directly shaping the livability and sustainability of urban areas. Fully understanding the spatial heterogeneity of heat exposure and its driving factors is therefore a vital prerequisite for climate-adaptive urban planning. However, most planning-oriented studies rely on land surface temperature (LST), and whether LST adequately represents human heat exposure and how it differs from physiologically relevant heat stress remains insufficiently examined. Here, adopting Landsat-retrieved 30-m LST and GPU-accelerated 1-m universal thermal climate index (UTCI) in Singapore, this study establishes a comprehensive “Modeling-Comparing-Assessing” framework to systematically evaluate the spatial and mechanistic discrepancies between the two metrics. We further investigate pronounced non-stationary and threshold-based quantitative relationships of the two metrics with urban factors by employing a novel geographically weighted XGBoost (GW-XGBoost) and generalized additive model (GAM) workflow. Our results demonstrate notable discrepancies in spatial patterns of LST and UTCI, along with substantial spatial heterogeneity in how 2D and 3D urban factors impact these two thermal metrics, as revealed by explainable GW-XGBoost models (the test R 2 = 0.855 for LST and 0.905 for UTCI, respectively). Crucially, spatially explicit SHAP interprets that sky view factor plays a central role in explaining UTCI variability but exhibits a comparatively marginal independent contribution to LST, indicating that LST inadequately captures shading-driven and radiative processes governing actual human heat stress. Notably, SHAP-GAM analysis indicates that higher albedo is associated with increased UTCI. These novel findings provide model-informed planning implications for integrating physiologically relevant thermal indices to support targeted heat risk management and climate-adaptive urban planning.

verified_metadata.title: Nonlinear driving mechanisms of land surface temperature under the coupling of blue-green space and urbanization: An analysis based on explainable machine learning
verified_metadata.abstract: Urban thermal stress has intensified under climate change and rapid urbanization. Blue-green space (BGS) is a key form of ecological infrastructure for mitigating urban heat; however, its thermal effects are jointly shaped by landscape patterns, urbanization intensity, and development-stage differences. Using Zhengzhou, China, as a case study, this study integrated blue-green space–urbanization coupling with interpretable land surface temperature (LST) modelling by combining coupling coordination degree (CCD) classification, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) attribution, robustness tests, and breakpoint validation. The results showed that CCD increased continuously from 2003 to 2023 and exhibited a clustered spatial pattern, with higher values in the urban core and lower values in the suburban fringe. The dominant drivers of LST varied across CCD gradients. In the low-coordination gradient, the primary model-attributed driver shifted from built-up percentage (BP) to forest percentage (FP), whereas in the middle- and higher-coordination gradients, water percentage (WP) and population density (POP) generally showed stronger contributions to model predictions. Nonlinear response analysis indicated that the effects of key blue-green-space and urbanization indicators were stage-dependent rather than governed by fixed thresholds. Fractional vegetation cover (FVC) exhibited the most consistent model-derived response interval, with nonlinear changes concentrated around 0.55–0.63 in the middle and later periods. BP showed later-stage warming-related warning intervals, mainly around 0.79–0.81, in middle- and higher-coordination gradients. WP showed weaker temporal stability, with a case-specific response interval around 0.17 observed mainly in the 2023 higher-coordination gradient. These findings provide case-based, model-derived evidence for differentiated heat-mitigation strategies in Zhengzhou and offer a methodological reference for testing similar coupled urban systems elsewhere.

verified_metadata.title: Assessing urban waterlogging risk and nonlinear drivers in high density cities: A multi model machine learning comparative approach
verified_metadata.abstract: Under the combined pressures of climate change and rapid urbanization, high density cities are facing increasing risks of urban waterlogging (UW) during extreme rainfall events. However, existing UW risk assessments often lack systematic comparisons of different machine learning models and provide limited insight into nonlinear driving mechanisms. Taking Shenzhen, a representative high density city in China, as a case study, this research develops an integrated assessment framework that combines multi source spatial data, multi model machine learning comparison, and explainable artificial intelligence techniques. Thirteen risk factors are selected from the perspectives of hazard, environmental susceptibility, and exposure. Four ensemble tree-based models, namely Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree, Extreme Gradient Boosting, and Light Gradient Boosting Machine, are applied and compared for UW risk prediction. The results show that the RF model achieves the best overall performance, with high-risk areas identified by the model covering 92.45% of historical UW locations. Spatially, UW risk in Shenzhen exhibits a pronounced southeast low and northwest high pattern, closely associated with highly urbanized and densely populated areas. Model SHAP and PDP analyses further reveal strong nonlinear and threshold effects among key risk factors. Impervious surface area, population density, and GDP are identified as the most influential factors associated with UW risk. In particular, road density shows a pronounced U-shaped relationship with UW risk, highlighting the dual role of road systems in drainage organization and impervious surface expansion. Overall, this study provides a transferable framework for resilience governance and spatial optimization in high density cities.

verified_metadata.title: Where could urban tree canopy expansion lower modeled summer cooling-energy demand? An equity-informed explainable machine-learning framework for Washington, DC
verified_metadata.abstract: Urban heat and rising summer cooling demand are increasingly important equity concerns in U.S. cities, yet fine-scale evidence on where urban greening may reduce summer cooling-energy demand remains limited. This study examines modeled summer cooling-energy demand across Census Block Groups (CBGs) in Washington, DC, with emphasis on the environmental and social conditions shaping neighborhood-scale cooling demand and the potential role of targeted tree-canopy expansion. We integrate indicators of tree canopy, imperviousness, planting opportunity, and neighborhood deprivation. Using spatially cross-validated XGBoost with a monotonic canopy constraint, SHAP-based interpretation, threshold identification, and counterfactual canopy scenarios, we identify where canopy intervention is most likely to provide benefit. Results show that modeled cooling demand is spatially concentrated in Wards 7 and 8, where higher deprivation, lower canopy, and less favorable built-environment conditions coincide. In contrast, Ward 3 exhibits the lowest deprivation, highest canopy, and lowest modeled cooling demand. Imperviousness alone does not fully explain modeled cooling demand: some areas show high imperviousness but relatively lower demand, suggesting that housing quality and broader socioeconomic advantage may condition the energy consequences of heat exposure. Areas with lower tree canopy tended to exhibit higher modeled cooling-energy demand, although this pattern varied with surrounding environmental and built-environment conditions. A model-derived canopy screening benchmark of approximately 21% in Wards 7 and 8 suggests that the strongest modeled cooling benefits are likely to occur in low-canopy neighborhoods below this benchmark. In both wards, about 64% of CBGs fell below the threshold. Planting opportunity emerges as the strongest implementation-relevant predictor. Overall, the findings provide an equity-centered framework for targeting urban greening to reduce modeled cooling-energy demand and support climate adaptation.

verified_metadata.title: SHAP-TAG: Operationalizing explainable AI for urban heat governance through attribution-severity typologies and policy triggers
verified_metadata.abstract: Urban heat adaptation increasingly relies on spatially explicit diagnostics, yet explainable AI outputs often remain difficult to translate into planning decisions. This study introduces SHAP-TAG (SHAP-based Typology and Actionable Governance), a framework that converts grid-level SHAP attributions into governance-ready products: attribution-severity typologies, model-based transition zones, and a tiered policy matrix. Using 30-m summer daytime land surface temperature (LST) modeling for the Greater Taipei Metropolitan Area, we distinguish a global diagnostic model from an urban action model to reduce topographic masking and focus interpretation on governance-facing built-environment drivers. The urban action model achieved a spatial cross-validation R² of 0.540 and MAE of 1.85°C using nine actionable variables. Compared with the global diagnostic model, NDVI became the dominant governance-facing signal in the urban action model, rising from rank 4 to rank 1 and showing a 2.31-fold increase in mean absolute SHAP magnitude. Full-urban SHAP clustering identified four attribution-severity tiers structured primarily by a vegetation-deficit and built-up-intensity gradient, with secondary modulation from openness and surface-composition signals: Strong vegetation–openness cooling core (10.73%), Moderate vegetation-cooling context (18.53%), Near-neutral transitional zone (33.35%), and Vegetation-deficit warming-priority zone (37.39%). These tiers are interpreted as a SHAP-calibrated governance sequence rather than four mutually independent heat mechanisms. NDVI showed a primary SHAP sign-change around 0.275 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.273–0.277), with the operational transition zone spanning approximately 0.27–0.33 when combined with sensitivity-based references. Albedo and sky-view-related indicators exhibited context-dependent attribution patterns and were therefore treated as operational references rather than universal physical thresholds. By linking attribution direction and magnitude, transition zones, and policy tiers, SHAP-TAG provides a locally calibrated but workflow-transferable approach for urban heat governance.

title: Smart point cloud–guided 3D gaussian splatting for urban modeling and data-driven analysis
abstract: This paper proposes a combined Smart Point Cloud (SPC) and Smart 3D Gaussian Splatting (S3DGS) framework for integrated urban analysis at block scale. Using laser-scanning point clouds and multi-view imagery of the aula–library heritage block in Netherlands, we first construct an SPC with CityGML-inspired semantics, then train a 3DGS model from the same image set and project SPC labels onto the Gaussians to obtain an S3DGS representation. On this basis, we derive a family of indicators that are usually produced in separate workflows: façade- and ground-plane composition from semantic projections; panoramic exposure metrics for greenery, buildings and sky from renderings of 3DGS with semantic labels (S3DGS); and column- and voxel-based statistics from the segmented SPC. The results demonstrate that the combined SPC–S3DGS model can simultaneously support plan-based, façade-based and view-dependent indicators, and can distinguish coherent scene types such as highly enclosed façade-adjacent zones, tree-dominated corridors, open plazas and mixed transitional spaces. Reflective surfaces and water, which are poorly captured by laser scanning, are recovered through the image-driven S3DGS component. We argue that SPC–S3DGS provides a generic semantic scene representation that can enrich urban digital twins with a visual–environment layer, and that it offers a promising basis for coupling structural, land-cover and exposure metrics in computational studies of computers, environment and urban systems.
